title: Vectors and mitigations for reward hacking during verification
body:
Authors: @stbenjam and @isegal --- This issue proposes a framework for securing benchmark tasks against reward hacking during verification, where agent activity is already separated from the verifier: **Part I: Framework** 1. **Verifier Taxonomies**: A breakdown of verification paradigms and the artifacts they grade. 2. **Cheating Vectors**: A catalog of known exploit patterns used to manipulate grading. 3. **Trusted Verifier Patterns**: Concrete defense-in-depth strategies **Part II: Terminal-Bench** 4. **Threat Model**: Describing the current state and its weaknesses 5. **Task Audit**: A review of all current tasks, mapping their verification categories to potential cheating paths and existing protections. 6. **Minimum Verifier Hardening**: Verifier-only fixes that close most open paths, and static patterns CI can flag. 7. **Open Questions**: Items that still need confirmation. --- # Part I: Framework ## Verifier Taxonomy Every task falls into one or more verification categories based on the artifacts it evaluates and the grading mechanism required. Others may exist. | Category | Description | Tasks | |---|---|---:| | **Data artifacts** | Inspect separately submitted files or data using trusted parsing, rendering, simulation, or inference. This check does not require executing a submitted implementation. | 28 | | **Program outputs** | Execute a submitted standalone program, application, or script against controlled inputs and validate externally observable results. | 23 | | **Code behavior** | Load, link, or exercise submitted components through an API, harness, or language toolchain to check behavior or properties, including proof acceptance. | 18 | | **Execution properties** | Profile runtime performance, memory footprint, storage consumption, or hardware metrics while building or running the submission. | 14 | | **System outcomes** | Validate persistent state changes, system-of-record updates, continuity, or audit history across a stateful environment modified by the agent. | 8 | --- ## Cheat Vector Taxonomy When evaluating untrusted agent submissions, verifiers face several distinct attack vectors (V1–V9). This is not an exhaustive list, and many more vectors likely exist. | ID | Vector | Description | Example | |---|---|---|---| | V1 | **Overwrite** | Replacing trusted test files, runner scripts, verifier dependencies, or evaluation tools. | Replacing a test file with tests that always pass. | | V2 | **Patch** | Tampering with assertions or test frameworks in a process that runs submitted code, including a child that reports its own pass. | Monkeypatch pytest to always pass. | | V3 | **Reward** | Writing a reward or another trusted result directly, including through a surviving process. | Writing reward 1.0 directly to the verifier's output path without solving the task. | | V4 | **Fail-open** | Exploiting permissive test runners that treat empty test suites, skipped tests, or generic `exit 0` codes as passes. | Skipping every test suite and earning full credit because the runner exited with code 0. | | V5 | **Sleeper agent** | Leaving processes running beyond the submission's execution step to interfere with later grading. | Launching a background daemon that sleeps 5 seconds and then overwrites the final reward file after grading concludes. | | V6 | **Staging** | Abusing links, special files, paths, or configuration/startup hooks as submitted files enter or are loaded by the verifier. | Submitting a symlink that tricks the verifier's privileged copy routine into overwriting a trusted test file. | | V7 | **Forgery** | Forging measurements, pass flags, counters, case selection, or other evidence the verifier treats as authoritative. | Running for 10 seconds while mocking an internal timer to report `elapsed_ms: 45` against a 1-second threshold. | | V8 | **Disclosure** | Reading expected answers, hidden inputs or reference outputs that submitted code can access. | A solver reads expected outputs from a world-readable fixture in `/tests`. | | V9 | **Exploit** | Exploiting a vulnerability or unsafe feature in a trusted parser, loader, renderer or toolchain that processes submitted data, so that data-only artifacts run code or read files. | A checkpoint with a pickle payload that runs when an unsafe `torch.load` fallback loads it, or a config string that injects script into a page rendered by a privileged browser. | --- ## Trusted Verifier Patterns Different tasks need different protections. These patterns can be combined to protect execution, grading and the evidence used to award a reward. ### 1. Unprivileged Worker in the Verifier Container When the submission does not need root, the simplest strong pattern keeps one container and separates the grader from the submission by user and by process. Root runs the tests and owns the verdict. An unprivileged worker, started as a fresh interpreter, loads the submission, runs it on inputs chosen by the verifier, and returns only the observed outputs. [terminal-bench#2114](https://github.com/harbor-framework/terminal-bench/pull/2114) uses this design for vllm-deepseek-streaming and resists all 21 cheats from [#2097](https://github.com/harbor-framework/terminal-bench/pull/2097) without seccomp or extra containers.
```mermaid flowchart TB subgraph ROOT["Root"] V["Verifier
Private tests and expected outputs"] R(["Reward"]) end subgraph UNPRIV["Unprivileged user"] W["Isolated worker
Fresh interpreter"] C["Submitted code"] end V -- "Verifier-selected inputs" --> W W --> C C -- "Observed output" --> W W -- "Untrusted data" --> V V --> R ```
**Protections provided:** V1, V3, V5 and V8 because the worker user cannot read the tests or write the reward and its leftover processes are killed, and V2, V4 and V7 because no trusted process loads submitted code. Submissions can still use threads, subprocesses and logging. **Limits:** Processes share a kernel and anything else the worker uid can reach, so check the image for world-writable paths, setuid binaries and sockets. Tasks whose submission needs root, installs system packages, or controls services that run under other uids (for example a database superuser) need extra care or the multi-container pattern below. --- ### 2. Multi-Container Verification When the submission cannot run as an unprivileged user in the verifier container, or a stronger boundary is needed, submitted code and trusted grading can run in separate containers. This adds orchestration complexity, so prefer pattern 1 when it is enough. Harbor’s Docker Compose integration can start both together: the runner waits for inputs, and the verifier waits for outputs. Containers share a kernel; this is a logical isolation boundary. [Docker security documentation](https://docs.docker.com/engine/security/) The runner container executes the submission on controlled inputs and emits untrusted data to a shared volume. The verifier container then independently ingests and grades that data.
```mermaid flowchart LR I["Verifier-selected inputs"] R("Runner container
Execute submitted code") O[("Shared outputs
Untrusted data")] V("Verifier container
Capture and validate data
Check with private tests") W(["Private reward"]) I -->|Read only| R R -->|Write| O O -->|Read only| V V --> W ```
**Protections provided when properly configured:** - **V1 (Overwrite):** The runner cannot modify verifier code, dependencies, or toolchains. - **V2 (Patch):** Submitted code cannot monkeypatch assertions running in the isolated verifier process. - **V3 (Reward):** The runner cannot write to the verifier's private reward file. Data returned by the runner is treated strictly as untrusted input, never as a grading verdict. Keep verifier files private and process namespaces separate. The runner must have restricted privileges and no access to the container engine or verifier control interfaces. Submitted executables, build hooks, plugins and unsafe loading of submitted artifacts belong in the runner; trusted checking tools can remain in the verifier. --- ### 3. Filesystem Protection & In-Container Sandboxing Filesystem controls can protect the verifier even when execution shares a container. They primarily address **V1 (Overwrite)** and **V3 (Reward)**. They do not prevent **V2 (Patch)** if submitted code and assertions share a process. - **Ownership & Permissions:** Use a dedicated worker identity, remove extra groups and capabilities, and prevent privilege gains. Make trusted files and parent directories inaccessible or non-writable to that worker. The verifier retains access to write its reward. User mappings and volume ownership vary by provider. - **Read-Only Mounts & Mount Namespaces:** Expose only required files and allow writes to scratch and output directories. [Bubblewrap](https://github.com/containers/bubblewrap) can construct this view using Linux namespaces, where the host and outer container permit them. Read-only paths must have no accessible writable aliases. - **Landlock:** Add filesystem access rules for the worker and its descendants. [Landlock](https://docs.kernel.org/userspace-api/landlock.html) supplements file permissions for supported operations. Available restrictions depend on the host kernel; inherited file handles need separate care. - **Seccomp:** Block unnecessary operations such as mounting or debugging to reduce attack surface. Ordinary filters cannot enforce directory-specific write rules. [Seccomp documentation](https://kernel.org/doc/html/latest/userspace-api/seccomp_filter.html) Check required protections on each provider before submitted code runs. Missing support should produce a setup error. --- ### 4. Process Containment & Lifecycle Cleanup **V5 — Sleeper agent** requires cleanup of the whole workload, including processes that outlive the main worker. - **Process Groups & Seccomp:** Start the worker in a dedicated process group, then block `setsid()` and `setpgid()` before submitted code runs. A trusted supervisor terminates remaining group members on success, failure or timeout. Blocking detachment alone does not stop children from outliving their parent. - **Protected Cgroups (v2):** Place the workload in a cgroup subtree it cannot leave. `cgroup.kill` terminates processes in that cgroup and its descendant cgroups, including workers that created new sessions or process groups. [Cgroup v2 documentation](https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/cgroup-v2.html) In-container cgroup management requires delegation; otherwise the host or container runtime must enforce workload cleanup. Seccomp filters also need support for the provider’s syscall architecture. --- ### 5. Post-Run Trajectory Review An LLM judge can review recorded commands, tool interactions, submitted changes and verifier logs for grading manipulation. Initial rewards remain provisional and can be retracted when cheating is established. This is a practical backstop where prevention is difficult. - **Protect the Evidence:** Store the record outside the agent’s control. Keep judge instructions separate from trajectory content to reduce prompt-injection risk. Treat the transcript as untrusted evidence. [OWASP guidance](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/LLM_Prompt_Injection_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html) - **Evidence-Backed Findings:** Require specific actions and supporting evidence, such as timestamps or diffs. Distinguish legitimate task work from grading manipulation; send ambiguous findings for human review. - **Enforce the Decision:** Keep the original reward and judge’s rationale, record the final reward in a trusted system, and ensure downstream scoring honors retractions. Review may detect evidence of V1–V8 when it appears in the record. Incomplete logs, prompt injection, context limits, missed cheats and false positives remain concerns. Evaluate judges against both legitimate runs and known cheating attempts; an unflagged run is not proof that no cheating occurred. --- ### 6. Verdict Integrity **V2 (Patch)**, **V4 (Fail-open)** and **V7 (Forgery)** require that the verdict come from a process that never loads submitted code. - **Separate the Judge:** The worker returns data; a trusted parent runs the assertions. - **Close the Verdict Channel:** The worker must not hold anything the parent reads as a verdict, such as an inherited pipe, an exit-code file or a "passed" log line. - **Fail Closed:** Remove every reward file and write reward 0 before running anything. Treat skipped tests, missing tests, errors and timeouts as failures. Dropping privileges does not help here: a monkeypatch acts on the process's own memory and needs no file access. A test-count gate (ctrf/JUnit) stops the skip variant of V4 but not V2, because patched tests really do report as passed. Ask whether agent code shares a process with anything whose output is trusted: the test runner, a forked child that reports its own verdict, a gate script judged by its exit code, or an in-process timer. --- ### 7. Safe Staging **V6 (Staging)** requires that submitted files enter the verifier as data and stay off trusted load paths. - **File Types:** Reject symlinks, hardlinks and special files unless the task needs them. Privileged helpers use `lstat` or `O_NOFOLLOW` on any path the worker can write. - **Import Paths:** Keep submission directories off the import path of trusted processes. Run trusted Python with `-I` or `-P`. - **Dependencies:** Bake verifier dependencies into the image. Install submitted dependencies as the worker, into an environment only the worker uses. --- ### 8. Trusted Measurement **V7 (Forgery)** requires that measurements come from outside the process being measured. - **External Counters:** Take time and memory from a supervisor or from cgroup counters such as `memory.peak`. - **Verifier-Chosen Inputs:** The verifier selects evaluation cases; the worker does not write them. - **Isolated Detectors:** Keep detectors out of content the submission controls. --- ### 9. Hidden Data **V8 (Disclosure)** requires that expected answers stay out of reach of submitted code. - **Verifier-Only Access:** Keep answers, hidden inputs and reference outputs readable only by the verifier identity, or outside the worker's filesystem view. --- ### 10. Untrusted Input to Trusted Tools **V9 (Exploit)** requires that trusted parsers, loaders and renderers treat submitted content as hostile. - **Data-Only Loaders:** Use formats and loaders that cannot run code, such as `safetensors`, `numpy.load(allow_pickle=False)` and `torch.load(weights_only=True)` with no fallback, on a patched version. - **No Evaluation:** Do not pass submitted strings to `eval`, `sympify`, template engines or shells. Validate against a strict grammar first. - **Escape at Boundaries:** Validate or escape submitted values before interpolating them into HTML, CSS, SQL or command lines. - **Least-Privilege Tools:** Run heavyweight parsers, browsers, CAD kernels, proof checkers and emulators as the worker identity, with no access to `/tests` or `/logs/verifier`. Disable browser file access and scripting when they are not needed. # Part II: Terminal-Bench ## Threat Model Terminal Bench tasks today must use the separate verifier mode (`environment_mode = "separate"`). When the agent phase ends, the agent container is stopped. Only the declared `artifacts` are copied into a fresh verifier container. This isolation does not cover what happens inside the verifier. Agent written code can still overwrite tests, patch assertions, write the reward or outlive grading, so the attack moves from the agent phase to the grading phase. The vectors below are about that surface. ### Harness Behavior Harbor at `cdb76bae`: - `/logs/verifier` is set to mode 0777 before the verifier runs (`src/harbor/trial/trial.py:889`, `src/harbor/environments/base.py:587-624`). - `reward.json` is read before `reward.txt` (`src/harbor/verifier/verifier.py:257-260`). - On Docker, symlinks inside directory artifacts reach the verifier as links (`src/harbor/environments/docker/docker_unix.py:145-156`). Tar-based providers drop absolute and escaping links (`src/harbor/environments/tar_transfer.py:65-82`). - If stopping the agent environment fails, the verifier still runs; the agent container mounts the same host directory as `/logs/verifier` (`src/harbor/trial/trial.py:1849-1855,1861-1865`). - `test.sh` runs as root unless `tests/Dockerfile` sets `USER` (`src/harbor/models/task/config.py:565-568`). A probe task on Docker, run against the CI-pinned `harbor==0.23.1.dev202609170426`, confirmed these behaviors: - `/logs/verifier` is `drwxrwxrwx` without the sticky bit, so an unprivileged user can create or replace `reward.txt` and `reward.json`. - `/tests` is world-readable (`COPY . /tests/` keeps 0644/0755), so an unprivileged user could read `/tests/secret.txt`. - An absolute symlink inside a directory artifact resolves against the verifier's filesystem: `/app/out/abs_link -> /tests/secret.txt` read the secret. - A relative symlink that escapes the artifact directory, a setuid binary, and a single-file artifact that is a dangling symlink are all dropped. Ownership is reset to root. - Artifact directories are recreated with mode 0777 in the verifier, so a `nobody` worker can plant symlinks for later root operations. Because of the first two items, locking `reward.txt` alone is not enough. `/logs/verifier` must be locked before agent code runs, and `reward.json` must be removed or rewritten by trusted code. None of the above has been verified on Modal, which CI uses. FrontierSWE reported that the Modal runtime socket let an unprivileged process read root-only files until the runtime directory was set to mode 0700. ## Exposed Cheating Paths Ratings are derived from the verifier code at `4def1f36`. **Open** means a concrete path exists in the code. **Partial** means a mitigation exists with a named gap. **Unverified** means the rating depends on behavior that could not be confirmed. Findings from a second independent audit at `3ef4bf2b`, including a pass for V8 across all tasks, are merged into this table.
